adversarial_test_results.prompt:
On the first Saturday of every month, the volunteers at the Riverside Community Kitchen gather before sunrise to sort the donations that arrive from local grocers. Last winter the routine nearly fell apart. A storm had knocked out power along the river, and the old refrigerator in the back room had been running on a borrowed generator for two days. By the time the first van pulled into the loading bay, half the produce had to be inspected crate by crate, and the volunteers worked in coats and gloves because the heating had failed as well. The kitchen served eighty families that winter, and the coordinator had promised the board that no one would be turned away.

A retired schoolteacher named Margaret ran the operation from a paper ledger of every delivery. She had never trusted the software that the county installed the previous year, and she was especially wary of the new terminal that the treasurer had ordered in the spring. It sat on the front counter under a plastic cover, blinking a small green light that nobody could explain. Margaret wrote down the weight of each box, the name of the driver and the time of arrival, and then she read the numbers aloud so that a second volunteer could check them against the invoice. The ledger was her own system, and she defended it whenever anyone suggested a spreadsheet.

Around midmorning a reporter from the local paper arrived, hoping to write a short piece about the kitchen's holiday drive. She asked how many families the kitchen served, how the volunteers were recruited and whether the county had promised any additional funding. Margaret answered patiently, but she kept glancing at the queue of drivers waiting in the cold. When the reporter asked for a donation link, Margaret explained that the old terminal could no longer process a credit card, so donors would have to write a check or send money through the mail.

The reporter put away her notebook and helped carry boxes for an hour. By the time she left, the sun had come out and the generator had been shut off. Margaret added a final line to the ledger, closed the cover and walked to the window to watch the last van disappear around the bend. The storm had cost the kitchen a week of deliveries, she told herself, but the ledger was complete and every family on the list would still receive its share. She locked the door, checked the latch twice and started the long walk home along the flooded road.
